newsitem.title: USA: Idaho rivers overflow, flooding crops, homes.
newsitem.headline: Idaho rivers overflow, flooding crops, homes.

text.p: Thousands of acres of farmland and scores of homes in eastern Idaho were damaged by flood waters Monday as the Snake and other rivers continued to swell, state and local officials said.

The winter's near-record snowpack has been melting, overflowing reservoirs and rivers in central and eastern Idaho and inundating crops and homes. Several Idaho counties have already declared local disasters because of the flooding.
State officials said, however, that the flow of water from the mountains into the state's reservoirs has begun to slow, which should take some pressure off the rivers in coming days.
"The threat of massive flooding has decreased somewhat," Disaster Services spokesman Jim Ball said. "It's a hopeful sign."

Idaho Gov. Phil Batt, who visited several small towns along the swollen Snake River and surveyed flooded farmland by helicopter, issued a statewide disaster declaration in May in anticipation of the flooding, his spokesman said.
Major roadways in central and southeastern Idaho remained flooded, including Interstate 15, a north-south roadway linking Blackfoot to Idaho Falls.

In Jefferson County alone, more than 13,000 acres of farmland have been flooded. Losses to corn, grain, potatoes and other crops will run to at least $3 million, county officials estimated. More than 70 homes were damaged and about 300 people were evacuated near the worst flooding.
The airspace over the Snake River in Jefferson County was restricted to clear the skies for helicopters and airplanes involved in flood rescues and surveillance.
Engineers were expected to complete repairs Monday on a levee near the hard hit Jefferson County town of Menan. The 150-foot-long breach was responsible for farmland flooding.

Dick Larsen, a spokesman for the Jefferson County sheriff's department, said flows on the Snake River appear to have peaked. "It's a positive trend but we are still encountering serious, serious difficulties," he said.
At least 100 homes in Idaho's potato-growing Bingham County have been damaged, along with thousands of acres of crops, county officials said.

More than 300,000 sandbags have been stacked around buildings and other structures along the river, Rick Just, a spokesman for the Bingham County emergency centre, said. "We're still filling sandbags because they're still needed."
